source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Scaling Into and Out of a Trade

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: ScaleInWithTrendOnContinuedPullback
candidates.quote: Into longs as a pullback falls further (pullbacks are small trends and therefore are in channels)... if there is a steeply rising moving average, bulls will scale into longs on a pullback below the moving average.
candidates.description: Add a further with-trend unit to an already-open long each time the pullback extends to a new low (a new lower low within the pullback channel) while the larger trend context is still believed valid.
candidates.book_order_type: additional buy limit/stop at each new pullback extreme

complexity.reason: the engine models one all-or-nothing position; adding independently-tracked units on continued adverse or favorable movement is not supported

notes: Recorded per the mining brief's instruction to keep scaling-in candidates even though the engine has no multi-unit position model.

candidates.name: ScaleInCountertrendAtFixedIntervalsFadingRangeExtreme
candidates.quote: I have a friend who is an expert at scaling into countertrend trades in channels... he would start to short on limit orders at the most recent swing high, and add to his position at the next one or two new highs in the channel, as long as each new entry was at least two points higher than the prior.
candidates.description: Fade the extreme of a channel or trading range with multiple countertrend units, adding another unit each time price makes a new extreme at least a fixed point/tick distance beyond the prior entry -- reliable only when the day/channel is not a strong trend.
candidates.book_order_type: additional sell limit at each new swing high at least minIntervalPoints above the prior entry

complexity.reason: needs both a multi-unit position (not modeled) and a 'not a strong trend day' context classification this chapter leaves undefined

candidates.name: AvoidScalingInAgainstStrongTrend
candidates.quote: Finally, it is risky to scale in against any strong trend... When a channel is strong, you should never scale in against the trend.
candidates.description: Block any countertrend scale-in (adding to, or newly entering against, a position) whenever the prevailing trend is judged strong.
candidates.pseudocode:
// research: 'strong trend' classification is not reduced to a bar-level test in this chapter
blockCountertrendScaleIn = strongTrendContext[0] && isCountertrendEntry[0];
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (blocks a countertrend scale-in/entry signal from being taken)

complexity.reason: "strong trend" has no stated bar-level test in this chapter; needs the same always-in/trend-strength design decision flagged elsewhere in this corpus

notes: Same underlying idea as R30-03 (avoid countertrend scalps in a strong trend), applied here specifically to scaling in.

candidates.name: AvoidScalingInLastHourOfDay
candidates.quote: it is risky to scale in against a trend in the final hour or so of the day, because you will too often find yourself holding a large losing position that you will have to cover by the close. Time is against you.
candidates.description: Block countertrend scale-in entries during the final hour or so of the trading session.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (blocks a countertrend scale-in signal from being taken late in the session)

complexity.reason: a plain time-of-day comparison, but combined with an is-countertrend-entry classification and the multi-unit scale-in context the engine does not model

notes: The time-of-day gate alone maps cleanly to the corpus's existing TimeWindow rule; the countertrend/scale-in qualifier is what makes this a distinct, harder candidate.

candidates.name: ExitOnSecondAdverseSignalAfterScalingIn
candidates.quote: Whenever you scale in against a trend, as a general rule you should exit if the market makes a second move against you. This means that if you are bottom picking in a bear trend and the market forms a low 2 short, especially if it is near the moving average and has a bear signal bar, you should exit your longs and even consider reversing to short.
candidates.description: After having scaled into a countertrend position, exit the entire combined position (and consider reversing) as soon as a second opposing setup forms against it.
candidates.book_order_type: exit at the market (or on a stop below the second adverse signal bar)

complexity.reason: needs both a persistent 'this position was built by countertrend scaling in' flag and a count of qualifying adverse setups since the scale-in, neither of which the engine currently tracks

candidates.name: WidenCombinedStopToTwiceInitialOnScaleIn
candidates.quote: if you were buying a pullback in a bull trend... and were thinking about using a 30 cent stop, you might instead buy more at that price and place a protective stop on your entire position 30 cents lower, or 60 cents below your first entry.
candidates.description: When adding a second unit at the level where the original stop would have been, widen the protective stop on the entire combined position to roughly twice the original single-unit stop distance, measured from the average entry price.
candidates.pseudocode:
// research: recomputing a stop from an average entry price across multiple units is a multi-unit position feature the engine does not model
averageEntryPrice = weightedAverage(unitEntryPrices, unitSizes); combinedStopDistance = stopMultiple * originalSingleUnitRiskDollars; exitLongStop = ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && low[0] <= averageEntryPrice - combinedStopDistance;
candidates.book_order_type: protective stop on the combined position placed at roughly twice the original single-unit risk below the average entry price

complexity.reason: requires an average entry price and a combined stop across multiple units, a multi-unit position feature the engine does not model

candidates.name: ScaleInJustBeyondObviousStopRunLevel
candidates.quote: The market often hits obvious protective stops to the tick and then reverses... an astute trader looking to scale in would have placed a limit order to short more at 11 ticks above the first entry, one tick below the three-point stop.
candidates.description: Place an additional (or reversal) entry one tick beyond the round-number/obvious stop distance from the original signal, on the premise that a cluster of other traders' stops sits exactly there and the market often runs them before reversing.
candidates.pseudocode:
// research: identifying the 'obvious'/round-number stop distance that other traders are using is a discretionary read of typical stop sizing for the current price action, not a stated bar-level test
obviousStopDistance = typicalStopDistanceForContext(); scaleInPrice = originalSignalPrice - (obviousStopDistance - tick); allowScaleInShort = high[0] >= scaleInPrice;
candidates.book_order_type: limit order to add to the position one tick inside the obvious round-number stop level

complexity.reason: the entry arithmetic (one tick beyond a distance) is trivial, but 'the obvious/appropriate stop size for the recent price action' is a discretionary judgment this chapter does not reduce to a formula, and adding a unit is a multi-unit feature the engine does not model

candidates.name: ScaleOutAtFixedDollarIntervals
candidates.quote: Other traders take partial profits at fixed intervals, like every 20 cents.
candidates.description: Take a partial profit on the open position every time open profit advances by a fixed additional increment, repeating for the life of the trade.
candidates.book_order_type: a ladder of profit-taking limit orders spaced at fixed dollar/tick intervals above the entry

complexity.reason: requires partial/multi-unit exits and a running count of intervals already filled, neither of which the engine models

candidates.name: ReAddScalpedContractOnNextSpikeBarClose
candidates.quote: you would have scalped out one contract during bar 5. On the close of bar 5, you could put your scalp contract back and once again be short two contracts.
candidates.description: During an ongoing spike, immediately re-enter (at the close of the very next bar) the unit that was just scalped out for a quick profit, restoring the position to its prior combined size.
candidates.pseudocode:
// research: tracking a just-scalped-out unit and immediately re-adding it is multi-unit position bookkeeping the engine does not support
justScalpedOutUnit = unitScalpedOutThisBar[0]; reenterShort = justScalpedOutUnit && isStrongBearTrendBar[0];
candidates.book_order_type: re-enter at the close of the spike bar that follows a scalped-out unit

complexity.reason: requires tracking a partially-closed multi-unit position and re-adding a unit within the same ongoing spike, which the engine does not model

candidates.name: PressWithTrendOnEachSpikeBarClose
candidates.quote: Many traders quickly add to their longs as the spike rapidly grows, bar after bar... Traders and institutions continued to buy relentlessly... They were scaling in all the way up.
candidates.description: Add a further with-trend unit at the close of every consecutive strong trend bar while a spike is underway ('pressing' a winning trade).
candidates.book_order_type: add to the position at the close of each qualifying strong trend bar

complexity.reason: the bar classification is trivial, but adding successive with-trend units to an open position is a multi-unit feature the engine does not model

candidates.name: BreakevenStopOnFirstUnitAfterAddingSecond
candidates.quote: you could short two more there and then be short three contracts, which is more than your usual risk, but put a breakeven stop on your first contract so that your total risk is the same as your usual total risk.
candidates.description: When adding units beyond the normal position size, move the protective stop on the earlier unit(s) to breakeven so the combined position's total dollar risk stays at the trader's usual level.
candidates.pseudocode:
// research: independently stopping different units of the same position (some at breakeven, others at their own risk level) is a multi-unit feature the engine does not model
exitFirstUnitLong = ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && unitCount[0] > normalUnitCount && low[0] <= firstUnitEntryPrice[0];
candidates.book_order_type: protective stop on the first unit moved to its own entry price (breakeven) once additional units are added

complexity.reason: requires tracking multiple units of one position with independently placed stops, a feature the engine does not model

candidates.name: DollarCostAverageFixedCalendarInterval
candidates.quote: an investor has some cash and wants to buy stock, he might use 10 percent of the cash to buy on the first of each of the next 10 months, regardless of whether the later entries are at a lower price.
candidates.description: Buy a fixed fraction of available capital at a fixed calendar interval (e.g., the first trading day of each month), regardless of price -- classic dollar cost averaging.
candidates.book_order_type: market buy for a fixed fraction of available capital on a fixed calendar schedule

complexity.reason: the calendar condition alone is trivial, but allocating a fixed fraction of capital across several scheduled entries independent of price is not something the engine's single-position model exposes

notes: Included for completeness since the book cites it explicitly as a scaling analogy, though it is really a capital-allocation policy rather than a price-action trading rule.

rejected.quote: make sure to keep your initial positions small enough so that the risk on your final position is within your usual tolerance... you need to keep your total risk within your normal range.
rejected.reason: position-sizing/capital-allocation guidance, not a bar-level entry/exit test

rejected.quote: You never know the probability with certainty, but you usually know when it is 60 percent or greater; if you are uncertain, then assume that it is 50 percent.
rejected.reason: a subjective probability estimate with no stated bar-level test

rejected.quote: suppose you believe that the chance that a stock now trading at $20 will fall to zero is 1 percent or less so you then buy 100 shares of a stock; if you scale in at each $5 drop...
rejected.reason: a cautionary illustrative example about a bad use of capital, not a stated trading rule; explicitly presented by the author as something to avoid

chapter_summary: This entire chapter is about scaling into and out of positions -- adding units with the trend on continued pullbacks or spikes, fading channel/range extremes with countertrend units, widening or re-averaging stops across multiple units, partial profit-taking at fixed intervals, and dollar cost averaging. Per the mining brief's explicit instruction, every candidate here is recorded even though the engine models a single all-or-nothing position with one stop, so nearly all of them are graded 'research' with the multi-unit limitation stated plainly in the reason; the two exceptions are context filters that reduce cleanly to existing primitives once the multi-unit wrapper is set aside (R31-03/AvoidScalingInAgainstStrongTrend, a trend-strength gate, and R31-04/AvoidScalingInLastHourOfDay, a time-of-day gate close to the corpus's existing TimeWindow rule). The bulk of the chapter's figures (31.1-31.8) are worked bar-by-bar scaling examples of the same handful of general ideas above and were not separately mined.
